title: Same Diwali Hamper Price, Fewer Pistachios as Dry Fruit Costs Soar
excerpt: Pistachio prices are up 30-40% and almonds about 20%, so retailers are holding hamper prices steady while quietly rebalancing boxes toward cashews, raisins and makhana.
body:
• Pistachios are up 30-40% and almonds about 20% over the past year, according to the Nuts and Dry Fruits Council of India, pushing the overall festive basket roughly 10% higher.
  • Retailers are holding hamper prices steady but cutting volume — the same box at the same price now carries fewer premium nuts.
  • Gift boxes are being rebalanced toward cashews, raisins and makhana, which are holding at last year's prices, with pistachios and almonds used as a premium topping.
  • If you are sending a hamper to family in India this Diwali, compare the nut mix and weight, not just the box price — a flat price tag can hide a smaller share of pistachios and almonds.

The Diwali gift box arriving at your door this year may look identical to last year's — same ribbon, same price tag, same festive packaging. Open it, and the difference shows. The pistachios and almonds that once filled the box are now a thinner layer on top, while cashews, raisins and makhana take up more of the space, according to reporting by The Hindu BusinessLine.

Dry fruits are the backbone of Diwali gifting in India. This year, a sharp rise in the price of the two most premium items — pistachios and almonds — is forcing sellers to quietly re-engineer what goes inside.

The Price Squeeze, Item by Item

The increases have been uneven, and that unevenness is exactly what is reshaping the boxes. "Over the past year, the rise in prices of dry fruits has been uneven. Pistachios are up by 30-40 per cent, almonds by around 20 per cent and dates, pecans and pumpkin seeds by 5-10 per cent. Cashews, walnuts, raisins and makhanas are holding at last year's levels. Taken together, the festive basket is likely to cost about 10 per cent more," said Gunjan Vijay Jain, President of the Nuts and Dry Fruits Council of India (NDFC-I).

"Retailers are keeping the prices unchanged but are cutting the volume."

— Trade source, speaking to The Hindu BusinessLine

Other industry estimates put the top end higher still. Trade reporting compiled by FreshPlaza puts in-shell pistachios 60-70% above last Diwali, with Peshawari pistachios — the variety used in Indian sweets — reaching a record ₹4,000 per kg, and wholesale in-shell pistachio prices up nearly 74% year on year to ₹1,650 per kg. Cashews, by contrast, are up a modest 5-8% on those estimates, raisins 2-5% and dried figs 5-15%.

Why Supplies Tightened

The squeeze starts at origin. Rajeev Pabreja, Managing Director of Commodity Trading Corporation, told BusinessLine that pistachio production is down 40-50%, while almond output is down about 10%, with production in both Iran and the United States affected. Arrivals from Iran and Afghanistan — two of India's key supply routes — have been slow.

Freight has compounded the problem. "Arrivals from Iran and Afghanistan are slow. The freight charges are up 10 times from Iran. Flight charges cost ₹200-300 a kg. As a result, dry fruit prices are at least 20 per cent higher," Pabreja said. Californian almond shipments to India have also faced delays, and a weaker rupee has raised the landed cost of imports. The government's September 2025 cut in GST on nuts, from 12% to 5%, has not been enough to offset the higher import and transport costs.

Traders and retailers have absorbed part of the increase through thinner margins, Jain said, which is why the shelf impact is gentler than the headline figures suggest.

How the Hamper Is Changing

The trade's answer is substitution, not sticker shock. Corporate and general trade demand remain good, according to trade sources cited by BusinessLine, but sellers are protecting the price point by adjusting the recipe: more of the nuts holding steady — cashews, raisins, makhana — and a surface layer of pistachios and almonds to keep the premium look. Quick-commerce platforms are seeing the same shift, with pumpkin seeds and even edamame appearing in gift boxes.

Cashew consumption may rise around 10% this season as buyers trade across, Jain said. For households, the practical effect is simple: a hamper bought at last year's price is not last year's hamper. Checking the stated weight and the proportion of pistachios and almonds matters more than the design on the lid.

What Happens After Diwali

There is some relief in the trade's outlook. The new almond crop should bring rates down by 5-10% after Diwali, walnut supply is strong, and Jain expects overall festive value to stay close to last year even as volumes adjust. For diaspora families ordering hampers for delivery to relatives in India the advice from this season's numbers is to order by contents and weight rather than by box size, because the rebalancing, not the price tag, is where this year's inflation is hiding.
